To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(-1,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x+1)^2+y^2=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = -2\cos\theta.$

- For $x=-1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-1 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ r & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta.$ Our curves intersect at the point $(-1,1).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\pi,$ as depicted below.  

![](images/76/769c13bea2dfc91aa3a507df1b7a763ae0da7591e0d6ba5face12268efb88240.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: -\sec\theta \leq r \leq -2\cos\theta, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq {\pi} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }{\int }_{-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /4}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{-\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157299 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-45cc9fce-954c-547e-835b-7dec4ec6d636"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186157103 :question/worked-solution "We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\dfrac{1}{2}$ centered at $\left(0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\!.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $x^2+\left( y-\dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2=\dfrac14,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = \sin\theta.$

- For $y=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta.$ Our curves intersect at the point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/12/1284a8b4b3f1634b4f7586d40ab8adf9cf93c69484b7ed069f138c8055e88892.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{2}\csc\theta \leq r \leq \sin\theta, \: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-ff6bf6f1-3574-59b2-8046-e358528c7f1f" :question/id #uuid "ff6bf6f1-3574-59b2-8046-e358528c7f1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-83946" :question/problem "![](images/31/31054ef4614814dd1c9131192504ea37f3527af75d8292fbce943c16235c9303.png)

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $1$ centered at $(1,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -1)^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} & =1 \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +1+{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .$

- For $x=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =1 \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ r & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is a washer enclosed between two circles centered at $(0,0)$ with radii $1$ and $2,$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/47/4752982aaf806b9e3b9c4d28d7a92bd01c3ff6a68afcca4235061a01b2fbc86f.png)

The easiest way to solve this problem is to convert it to polar coordinates. Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/e0/e0cc6c7f92704365c3ce15b91d85f703330b767a01f1f773b014cf61620563a3.png)

             

The change of variables formula for polar coordinates states 

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 7 \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}} = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158487 :tutorial/content "Let's get some more practice at expressing regions in polar coordinates.

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is a washer enclosed between two circles centered at $(0,0)$ with radii $1$ and $2,$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/47/4752982aaf806b9e3b9c4d28d7a92bd01c3ff6a68afcca4235061a01b2fbc86f.png)

The easiest way to solve this problem is to convert it to polar coordinates. Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/e0/e0cc6c7f92704365c3ce15b91d85f703330b767a01f1f773b014cf61620563a3.png)

             

The change of variables formula for polar coordinates states 

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 7 \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}} = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186158487 :tutorial/content "Let's get some more practice at expressing regions in polar coordinates.

To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\dfrac{1}{2}$ centered at $\left(0,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\!.$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For $x^2+\left( y-\dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2=\dfrac14,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2})}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $r$ cannot be identical to zero on the entire semicircle, we must have $r = \sin\theta.$

- For $y=\dfrac{1}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta.$ Our curves intersect at the point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$ So, the entire region lies between the radial lines $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as depicted below.  

![](images/12/1284a8b4b3f1634b4f7586d40ab8adf9cf93c69484b7ed069f138c8055e88892.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ as 

$$
\Delta = \Big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: \dfrac{1}{2}\csc\theta \leq r \leq \sin\theta, \: \dfrac{\pi}{4} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2} \Big\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {\int }_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta [r]_{1/2\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }^{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )]_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186157616 :question/id #uuid "2616ffa6-4ad5-55b3-bbe1-ee00aff863bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-161102"} {:db/id 17592186157840 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to compute the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is a washer enclosed between two circles centered at $(0,0)$ with radii $1$ and $2,$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/47/4752982aaf806b9e3b9c4d28d7a92bd01c3ff6a68afcca4235061a01b2fbc86f.png)

The easiest way to solve this problem is to convert it to polar coordinates. Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/e0/e0cc6c7f92704365c3ce15b91d85f703330b767a01f1f773b014cf61620563a3.png)

The change of variables formula for polar coordinates states 

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 7 \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}} = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}.

Consider the region enclosed by the curve $x^2+(y-2)^2=4$ and the line $y=2,$ as shown below.

![](images/df/dffcd94cc96c33d173704a63cb03fb0f0098bc67d6c66a855c16f59694bde8e1.png)

This region represents a portion of the disk of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2).$

First, we recall the usual transformations from polar to Cartesian coordinates:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Let's now use the above formulas to write the functions that bound our region in polar coordinates:

- For $x^2+(y-2)^2 = 4,$  we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =4 \\ (r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta -2)^{2} & =4 \\ ({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}\theta -4r\operatorname{sin}\theta +4 & =4 \\ {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )-4r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ {r}^{2}-4r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =0 \\ r(r-4\operatorname{sin}\theta ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2 \\ r\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =2 \\ r & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}\theta } \\ r & =2\operatorname{csc}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/b0/b09ab4e4e08dfb056964947dc866b965940b761d70c945faf001446c1df7869f.png)

$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "870d0884-b353-5292-b2e5-593725024502" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4472 :tutorial/title "Writing More Complex Regions in Polar Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "098b5c2c-68e3-5938-bf5f-621a688c8ba7" :step/math-academy-id 27531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158142}}] :activity/title "Double Integrals Between Polar Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186157490} {:db/id 17592186158141 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158486 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to compute the double integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}},
$$

 

where $D$ is a washer enclosed between two circles centered at $(0,0)$ with radii $1$ and $2,$ respectively, as shown below.

![](images/47/4752982aaf806b9e3b9c4d28d7a92bd01c3ff6a68afcca4235061a01b2fbc86f.png)

The easiest way to solve this problem is to convert it to polar coordinates. Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as

$$
x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta.
$$

The preimage of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ is the rectangular region $\Delta,$ given by 

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The region $D$ and its preimage $\Delta$ are shown below.

![](images/e0/e0cc6c7f92704365c3ce15b91d85f703330b767a01f1f773b014cf61620563a3.png)

The change of variables formula for polar coordinates states 

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dA & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}\theta +{sin}^{2}\theta )}\,r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating this integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta {\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,dr \\  & =2\pi \cdot {[\frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot [{2}^{3}-{1}^{3}] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 7 \\  & =\frac{14\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\iint\limits_{D}{{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,\mathrm d A}} = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "26614628-ce8b-5afe-ac90-b277c7c0f887" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4466 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0aaacbc4-1148-50d7-a5cf-50570ae0a925" :step/math-academy-id 27487 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158144}} {:db/id 17592186158486 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to compute the double integral
